cards.title: Memory has three doors
cards.body: Psychologists split memory into three stages. Sensory memory catches everything for a split second, short-term memory holds a handful of items for under a minute, and long-term memory stores things for years. Most of what you experience never makes it past the first door — and that's fine, it keeps you sane.

cards.title: Short-term memory is tiny
cards.body: Your short-term memory holds about 7 items, give or take 2 — a phone number, a grocery list, a stranger's name. It fades in 15 to 30 seconds unless you do something with it. This is why you walk into a room and forget why: the item dropped before it got stored anywhere.

Read this number: 8472916. Look away and try to repeat it backwards. Most people lose it after 4-5 digits. Now try chunking it: 847-29-16. Grouping turns 7 items into 3 chunks, and suddenly it fits. Phone numbers use this trick on purpose.

Getting something into long-term memory needs three things: attention (you actually noticed it), meaning (it connects to something you know), and repetition spaced over time. Highlighting a page gives you none of the three — that's why it feels productive and isn't.

cards.q: Why do you forget why you walked into a room?
choices: The item faded from short-term memory before it was stored
Your brain deleted it on purpose to save space
You never actually wanted to go there
cards.explain: Short-term memory fades in 15-30 seconds unless the item gets attention and encoding. Walk too slowly, get distracted once, and it's gone before it reaches long-term storage.

flashcards.front: What are the three stages of memory?
flashcards.back: Sensory memory, short-term memory, and long-term memory.

flashcards.front: Roughly how many items does short-term memory hold?

flashcards.back: Grouping items into fewer, bigger units so more fits in short-term memory (like 847-29-16 instead of 8472916).

flashcards.front: What three things move a memory into long-term storage?
flashcards.back: Attention, meaning (connection to what you know), and spaced repetition.

questions.q: Which memory stage holds information for years?
questions.explain: Sensory memory lasts a fraction of a second, short-term under a minute. Long-term memory is the archive — years to a lifetime.

questions.q: How long does an unrehearsed item last in short-term memory?
questions.explain: Without rehearsal it decays in 15-30 seconds. That's the window you have to do something with it — repeat it, write it down, or connect it to something.

questions.q: You remember 847-29-16 more easily than 8472916. What are you using?
questions.explain: Chunking groups items into fewer units, and memory counts chunks, not digits. Seven digits becomes three chunks — inside the limit.

questions.q: Which study habit actually builds long-term memory?
choices: Re-reading the chapter the night before
questions.explain: Spaced retrieval forces your brain to reconstruct the memory, which is what strengthens it. Re-reading and highlighting feel fluent but barely register.

questions.q: Why does paying attention matter for memory?
choices: Attention is the gate: unattended info never gets encoded
It doesn't matter, memory is automatic
questions.explain: Encoding requires attention. Information you never truly noticed never reaches short-term memory, let alone long-term storage.

cards.title: Your brain takes shortcuts
cards.body: Your brain makes thousands of decisions a day, so it uses mental shortcuts called heuristics. They're fast and usually right — but they misfire in predictable ways. Those predictable misfires are called cognitive biases, and everyone has them, including the experts warning you about them.

cards.title: Confirmation bias
cards.body: Confirmation bias is our habit of noticing and trusting information that agrees with what we already believe, while ignoring what doesn't. Two people can read the same news story and both walk away convinced it proved their point. The bias isn't in the story — it's in the reader.

Anchoring: a store lists a jacket at $400, then marks it down to $160. You feel like you saved $240 — even if the jacket was never worth $400. The first number you saw became the anchor, and every judgment after it drifted toward it.

You can't delete your biases, but you can build speed bumps: ask 'what would change my mind?', seek out the strongest opposing argument, and distrust decisions that feel too fast and too comfortable at the same time.

cards.q: You only read news from sources that agree with you. Which bias is that?
cards.explain: Confirmation bias favors information that confirms existing beliefs and filters out the rest. Anchoring is about first numbers; survivorship bias is about only seeing the winners.

flashcards.back: A predictable pattern where mental shortcuts (heuristics) misfire and distort judgment.
Favoring information that agrees with what you already believe, while ignoring what doesn't.
Over-relying on the first piece of information seen — like a $400 'original price' making $160 feel like a steal.

flashcards.front: Can you get rid of your biases?
flashcards.back: No, but you can build speed bumps: seek opposing views and ask what would change your mind.

choices: A fast mental shortcut the brain uses to decide quickly
questions.explain: Heuristics are quick rules of thumb. They save time and usually work — cognitive biases are the cases where they predictably don't.

questions.q: A negotiator opens with an absurdly high price. What are they exploiting?
questions.explain: The first number anchors the negotiation — every counteroffer gets pulled toward it, even when everyone knows the opener was ridiculous.

questions.q: After an election, everyone claims they 'knew it all along.' That's:
questions.explain: Hindsight bias makes past events feel more predictable than they were. Nobody actually knew — memory rewrites the uncertainty away.

questions.q: You fear plane crashes more than car crashes despite the statistics. That's the:
questions.explain: The availability heuristic judges probability by how easily examples come to mind. Plane crashes are vivid and newsworthy; car crashes are routine and forgettable.

questions.q: What's the most reliable defense against your own biases?
choices: Deliberately seek the strongest opposing argument
Trust your gut — it's usually right
Make decisions as fast as possible
questions.explain: You can't think your way out of a bias from inside it. Steel-manning the other side is the external check that actually works.

cards.title: Two kinds of fuel
cards.body: Motivation comes in two flavors. Intrinsic motivation is doing something because it's interesting or satisfying — playing guitar because you love the sound. Extrinsic motivation is doing it for a reward or to avoid punishment — practicing because your teacher checks. Both work, but they don't work the same way.

cards.title: Rewards can backfire
cards.body: Here's the twist: paying people for something they already enjoy can kill the enjoyment. Psychologists call it the overjustification effect. Once the reward becomes the reason, the activity feels like work — and when the reward stops, the behavior stops with it.

In a classic study, kids who loved drawing were paid for each drawing. They drew more while the payments lasted — then drew less than before once the payments stopped. The kids who were never paid just kept drawing. The reward rewrote their reason.

To stay motivated on long goals: make progress visible (checklists, streaks), shrink the next step until starting feels trivial, and protect the intrinsic part — do at least some of it just because you like it, with no reward attached.

choices: External rewards can reduce enjoyment of an activity you already liked
cards.explain: When a reward becomes the reason for doing something, the intrinsic interest fades. Remove the reward and the behavior often drops below where it started.

flashcards.back: Intrinsic: doing it because it's interesting. Extrinsic: doing it for a reward or to avoid punishment.
When external rewards reduce the enjoyment of something you already liked doing.

flashcards.front: Name three things that sustain motivation on long goals.
flashcards.back: Visible progress, tiny next steps, and protecting the intrinsic enjoyment.

flashcards.front: Why do streaks and checklists help?
flashcards.back: They make progress visible, which feeds motivation without replacing the intrinsic reason.

questions.q: Reading novels for fun, then getting paid per book and losing interest — that's:
questions.explain: The payment reframed reading as work. Intrinsic interest got crowded out, so when payments stopped, reading stopped too.
Curiosity comes from inside — the activity is its own reward. Bonuses and fear are extrinsic: reasons imposed from outside.

questions.q: What's the best first move on a goal you've been avoiding?
choices: Shrink the next step until starting feels trivial
questions.explain: Motivation usually follows action, not the other way around. A 2-minute first step gets you moving, and motion creates momentum.

questions.q: A student studies only to avoid failing. That's primarily:
questions.explain: Avoiding punishment is extrinsic — the reason comes from outside the activity itself. It works, but it's fragile and stressful.

questions.q: Why does visible progress (streaks, checklists) boost motivation?
choices: It proves effort is paying off, feeding the desire to continue
It replaces the need for any real goal
questions.explain: Humans are wired to continue things that show progress. A growing streak is evidence your effort matters — that's fuel.
